assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Assume a coloring f satisfies the circumcenter-closure hypothesis. Fix any point O and let c=f(O). Suppose some point G has the opposite color. Around the pair O,G, use L4 to build five auxiliary points X_i on the circle centered at G through O, each supported by a distinct pair A_i,B_i of points on the circle centered at O through G. By L2, the circle centered at O can contain at most two points of the color opposite to c; since the ten supporting points A_i,B_i are distinct, at least three support pairs are entirely colored c. For each such pair, L5 transfers color c from O to the corresponding X_i. Thus the circle centered at G contains three distinct points of color c. Applying L1 to those three points forces G itself to have color c, contradicting that G had the opposite color. Hence no opposite-colored point exists; all points have color c. This is exactly the root theorem.

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Fix an arbitrary coloring f satisfying the monochromatic-circumcenter hypothesis. Choose an arbitrary point O and call its color c. To prove the coloring is constant, assume there exists a point G of the other color. Let r=dist(O,G)>0 and choose the small radius s=r/4, so 0<s<r/2. By the finite geometric configuration lemma, we can select five distinct auxiliary points X_1,...,X_5 on the small circle centered at G of radius s, and for each X_i two support points A_i,B_i on the large circle centered at O of radius r, with all ten support points pairwise distinct and arranged so that X_i is the circumcenter of triangle O A_i B_i. Because the large circle is centered at O, the circle bound lemma implies that at most two of these ten support points can have the color opposite to c. A simple pigeonhole argument then gives at least three indices i for which both A_i and B_i have color c. For each such index, the color-transfer lemma shows that X_i must also have color c, because X_i is the circumcenter of the monochromatic triangle O A_i B_i. Thus the small circle centered at G contains three distinct points of color c. Applying the circle-center lemma to that circle forces G itself to have color c, contradicting the choice of G as opposite-colored. Therefore no opposite-colored point exists, so every point of the plane has color c. Since f was arbitrary, this proves the theorem.

Equivalently: ∀f [(∀A,B,C (noncollinear ∧ f(A)=f(B)=f(C) ⇒ f(circumcenter(A,B,C))=f(A))) ⇒ (∃c ∈ {red,green} ∀P f(P)=c)].

conclude: exists c in {red,green} such that forall P in R^2, f(P) = c

payload.theorem_nl: Suppose that each point in the plane is colored either red or green, subject to the following condition: For every three noncollinear points $A,B,C$ of the same color, the center of the circle passing through $A,B$ and $C$ is also this color. Prove that all points of the plane are the same color.

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Fix an arbitrary coloring f satisfying the monochromatic-circumcenter hypothesis. Assume for contradiction that both colors occur, and choose opposite-colored points O and G. Let r=dist(O,G)>0 and choose s=r/4, so 0<s<r/2. By the elementary circle lemma, choose seven distinct points on the circle centered at G with radius s. By the local exclusion lemma L8, that circle cannot contain five points of color f(G), so among the seven points at least three must have the other color, namely f(O). Those three distinct same-colored points lie on one circle centered at G, so L1 forces the center G itself to have color f(O), contradicting the choice of O and G as opposite-colored. Therefore both colors cannot occur, and the coloring is constant. The key improvement over the rejected attempts is that the heavy geometry is localized in L8 and uses the actual 2-coloring hypotheses; no false global statement about arbitrary circumcenter-closed subsets is used. Internally, L8 is supported by the corrected transfer lemma L3, the exact two-circle intersection lemma L4, the finite generic-position support configuration L5, the circle bound L2, and the pigeonhole lemma L6.

steps.derives: Fix an arbitrary coloring f : R^2 -> {red,green} satisfying the root hypothesis: for every noncollinear A,B,C in R^2, if f(A)=f(B)=f(C), then f(circumcenter(A,B,C))=f(A).
steps.trivial_justification: This is the assumption of the root theorem, specialized to an arbitrary coloring f.

steps.derives: Assume for contradiction that f takes both colors. Then there exist points O,G in R^2 such that f(O) ≠ f(G).
steps.trivial_justification: To prove the coloring is constant, it suffices to rule out the possibility that both colors occur. If both colors occur, choose one point O of one color and one point G of the other color.

steps.derives: The points O and G are distinct, so r := dist(O,G) satisfies r > 0.
steps.trivial_justification: If O=G then f(O)=f(G), contradicting A2. Distinct points in the Euclidean plane have positive distance, hence r>0.

steps.derives: Define s := r/4. Then 0 < s < r/2.
steps.trivial_justification: Since r>0, dividing by 4 gives s>0, and r/4<r/2 is immediate from positivity of r.

steps.derives: There exist seven pairwise distinct points X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4,X_5,X_6,X_7 on Circle(G,s).
steps.trivial_justification: Apply L7 to the point G and the positive radius s from A4.

steps.derives: Among the seven points X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4,X_5,X_6,X_7, at most four have color f(G).
steps.trivial_justification: Lemma L8 applies because A1 supplies the root hypothesis, A2 supplies the opposite-colored points O and G, and A4 gives 0<s<dist(O,G)/2. Therefore Circle(G,s) cannot contain five pairwise distinct points all of color f(G). Since the seven X_i are pairwise distinct and lie on that circle by A5, at most four of them can have color f(G).

steps.derives: At least three of the seven points X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4,X_5,X_6,X_7 have color different from f(G). Since the only two colors are red and green and f(O) ≠ f(G), those at least three points all have color f(O).
steps.trivial_justification: There are seven total points and at most four have color f(G), so at least three do not have color f(G). Because the codomain of f is exactly the two-element set {red,green}, any point not colored f(G) must be colored with the other color, namely f(O) from A2.

steps.derives: f(G)=f(O).
steps.trivial_justification: Choose three distinct points among the seven X_i that have color f(O), whose existence is given by A7 and whose distinctness is inherited from A5. These three points lie on Circle(G,s) by A5. Applying L1 with center G and radius s shows that the center G must also have color f(O).

steps.derives: Contradiction.
steps.trivial_justification: A2 states f(O) ≠ f(G), while A8 states f(G)=f(O).

steps.derives: Therefore f does not take both colors. Hence there exists a color c in {red,green} such that for every point P in R^2, f(P)=c.
steps.trivial_justification: From the contradiction, both colors cannot occur. Since every point has one of the two colors red or green, the image of f is a singleton subset of {red,green}. Let c be its unique element. Then every point P satisfies f(P)=c.

steps.derives: For every function f : R^2 -> {red,green}, if for all noncollinear points A,B,C in R^2 with f(A)=f(B)=f(C) we have f(circumcenter(A,B,C)) = f(A), then there exists a color c in {red,green} such that for every point P in R^2, f(P)=c.
